main.title: Gate of Thunder
main.subtitle: A fighter crossing seven battles
main.summary: Gate of Thunder is Red Company's side-scrolling shooter, released for PC Engine's Super CD-ROM² in Japan on 21 February 1992.

cards.heading: A fighter crossing seven battles
cards.text: Gate of Thunder is Red Company's side-scrolling shooter, released for PC Engine's Super CD-ROM² in Japan on 21 February 1992. Hawk pilots the Hunting Dog against an armada seeking the Starlight energy source, with Esty's Wild Cat providing support. Seven stages carry the ship through military opposition and large bosses. Its dense scenery and recorded rock music give the journey considerable force, while the player's immediate task remains clear: find a safe line through the fire and bring the next enemy into range.

cards.heading: Firepower that can face behind
cards.text: The Hunting Dog collects weapons and supporting firepower as the screen advances. Threats arrive from different directions, requiring attention to the space behind the ship as well as the formation ahead. Large enemies and stage obstacles break up that movement before each boss encounter. The ship's weapons provide ways to answer those changing arrangements, but positioning determines how safely an advantage can be used. Four difficulty settings alter the challenge, giving the same sequence of seven stages different demands as the player becomes more familiar with its patterns.

cards.heading: A showcase for the Super CD
cards.text: The team within Red Company included former Technosoft staff who had worked on Thunder Force, and later formed CAProduction. Nick Wood of Sound Design composed the score. Increased memory available through Super CD-ROM² supported the detailed presentation. In North America, Gate of Thunder accompanied the TurboDuo on a disc that also included Bonk's Adventure, Bonk's Revenge and Bomberman. That bundle made the shooter a prominent demonstration of the new hardware, with its fast action and recorded music immediately illustrating what the disc-based system could deliver.

main.title: Contra III: The Alien Wars
main.summary: Contra III: The Alien Wars is a 1992 run and gun video game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES).

cards.heading: Six stages of alien war
cards.text: Contra III: The Alien Wars is a 1992 run and gun video game developed and published by Konami for the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). It is the third home console entry in the Contra series after Contra (1988) and Super C (1990) for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). In PAL regions, it was retitled Super Probotector: Alien Rebels and the player characters were replaced with robots. The player is tasked with fighting off an alien invasion of Earth across six stages. Four stages feature side-scrolling action traditional to the series while two are presented from an overhead perspective. It is the first Contra title to have been directed by Nobuya Nakazato who later directed other games in the series. He designed Contra III to feature more comical elements, a more cinematic soundtrack, and tighter stage design than its predecessors.

cards.heading: The Super Nintendo original and its ports
cards.text: Contra III received positive reviews, with critics praising its arcade quality derived from its sound and visual design. It has been called one of the best Contra games in retrospective reviews and is considered one of the greatest video games of all time. It was ported to the Game Boy as Contra: The Alien Wars (1994) by Factor 5 where it received positive reviews for its Super Game Boy enhancements. Konami also released a Game Boy Advance port titled Contra Advance: The Alien Wars EX (2002) which received more critical reviews for removing features in the original. The Super NES version was rereleased several times including the Super NES Classic Edition, Contra Anniversary Collection, and various online distribution services.

main.title: Shining Force
main.subtitle: An army of individual stories
main.summary: Released in Japan on March 20, 1992, Shining Force brought a tactical role-playing adventure to Sega’s Mega Drive. A young swordsman from Guardiana faces the invasion of Runefaust and the threat surrounding the ancient Dark Dragon. Exploration and conversation connect the battles: towns provide equipment, information and potential recruits before the party returns to the field. Created by Climax and Sonic, the game turns a fantasy journey into a succession of encounters where moving a character into position matters as much as choosing an attack.

cards.heading: A journey measured in squares
cards.text: Released in Japan on March 20, 1992, Shining Force brought a tactical role-playing adventure to Sega’s Mega Drive. A young swordsman from Guardiana faces the invasion of Runefaust and the threat surrounding the ancient Dark Dragon. Exploration and conversation connect the battles: towns provide equipment, information and potential recruits before the party returns to the field. Created by Climax and Sonic, the game turns a fantasy journey into a succession of encounters where moving a character into position matters as much as choosing an attack.

cards.heading: Faces behind the formation
cards.text: The battlefield is divided into squares, but the soldiers are more than interchangeable pieces. Knights, archers, spellcasters and other recruits have different capabilities, making the composition and placement of the force part of the adventure. Sega’s original-game description highlights a cast of thirty warriors. Combat cuts from the map to close-up attack scenes, giving the small figures a second, theatrical presence. Masahiko Yoshimura’s music accompanies both the calm of towns and the march into battle. The combination makes tactical planning approachable through recognisable characters rather than an anonymous army.

main.title: Ultima VII: The Black Gate
main.summary: Ultima VII: The Black Gate is the seventh installment of the Ultima series of role-playing video games.

cards.heading: The Avatar returns to Britannia
cards.text: Ultima VII: The Black Gate is the seventh installment of the Ultima series of role-playing video games. It was published in April 1992 for MS-DOS by Origin Systems. The player returns as The Avatar, a would-be paragon of moral virtue who faces down many dangers and deceptions in order to cleanse the medieval fantasy world of Britannia of assorted plots and schemes, monster infestations, and the undermining of crown authority. A Super NES conversion was released in 1994.

cards.heading: Richard Garriott and the Black Gate
cards.text: The Black Gate was critically acclaimed and commercially successful, being widely lauded as a high point in the series and is also regarded as one of the best video games ever created. In an interview with GameSpot, Richard Garriott stated that Ultima VII "was the most masterfully executed of the Ultima series". He has also often stated that the game was, along with Ultima IV, his own favorite installment overall.

main.title: Panic Restaurant
main.subtitle: EIM · Nintendo Entertainment System
main.summary: Panic Restaurant is EIM's NES platformer about a chef reclaiming his restaurant after a rival's curse brings its food to life. In the overseas edition, Cookie fights through six stages with kitchen utensils before confronting Ohdove. Familiar ingredients become animated enemies, giving the setting an immediately understandable joke. A kitchen is supposed to be somewhere the chef controls what happens to the food. Here, the food fights back, and the tools used to prepare it become the equipment needed to survive.

cards.heading: Dinner has turned against the chef
cards.text: Panic Restaurant is EIM's NES platformer about a chef reclaiming his restaurant after a rival's curse brings its food to life. In the overseas edition, Cookie fights through six stages with kitchen utensils before confronting Ohdove. Familiar ingredients become animated enemies, giving the setting an immediately understandable joke. A kitchen is supposed to be somewhere the chef controls what happens to the food. Here, the food fights back, and the tools used to prepare it become the equipment needed to survive.

cards.heading: A kitchen utensil becomes a weapon
cards.text: The overseas Cookie begins with a pan, while further equipment changes how he deals with the restaurant's hazards. The stages build their action around food and the spaces where it would normally be prepared or served. That consistency helps the absurd enemies belong to the same world. A dangerous dish can still be recognised as dinner, even while it approaches like a conventional platform-game opponent. The visual humour depends on that quick recognition, letting an ordinary object acquire another role without needing an explanation.

cards.heading: A changed chef for the overseas menu
cards.text: Kenji Eno designed the game before becoming better known for D and Enemy Zero. The Japanese edition stars Kokkun, whose default attack uses his head; localisation replaced it with Cookie's pan and changed other weapons and names. Taito published the game, which arrived late in the NES's life. Its character comes from applying one comic idea consistently: a restaurant has become an obstacle course, and the person best equipped to put it right is still the chef with the familiar tools.

main.title: Kirby's Dream Land
main.subtitle: A small hero takes a deep breath
main.summary: HAL Laboratory’s 1992 Game Boy adventure introduced Kirby through a simple set of actions: inhale, spit out enemies and float through the air.

cards.heading: Inhale, float, explore
cards.text: Kirby’s Dream Land arrived on Game Boy in Japan on April 27, 1992, developed by HAL Laboratory and published by Nintendo. Its hero can inhale enemies and objects, then spit them back as projectiles. Holding a breath also lets Kirby float, making height something to explore rather than just an obstacle to clear with a precisely timed jump. These few actions give the character an immediately recognisable identity.

cards.heading: Before the Copy Abilities
cards.text: The original game does not yet give Kirby the Copy Abilities associated with later adventures. Instead, its movement and combat grow from swallowing, aiming and choosing when to float or return to the ground. Nintendo’s original description emphasises straightforward controls that let newcomers reach the ending. Jun Ishikawa’s music gives this compact monochrome adventure a melodic identity as clear as its round protagonist.

main.title: Treasure
main.subtitle: Treasure Treats Every Project as a Laboratory for a New Rule
main.summary: Treasure was founded on June 19, 1992 by developers many of whom came from Konami.

cards.heading: Treasure Treats Every Project as a Laboratory for a New Rule
cards.text: Treasure was founded on June 19, 1992 by developers largely drawn from Konami. Its games include Gunstar Heroes and Ikaruga, action projects built around distinctive weapon and scoring rules. The studio developed a reputation for compact games with dense encounters and frequent changes of pace.

cards.heading: Leaving Konami to work small
cards.text: Masato Maegawa recalled early Gunstar Heroes discussions taking place in cafés before the founders had chosen a company name. They began with action games, a field they already knew. Gunstar Heroes gained approval while the team also worked on McDonald's Treasure Land Adventure. Maegawa wanted Treasure's first published game to be an original project with the studio's own name visible at startup.

cards.heading: Gunstar Heroes and the density of action
cards.text: Gunstar Heroes offers four weapon types that can be combined into different attacks. A close-range choice encourages moving nearer, while homing shots let players give more attention to dodging. Grabs, throws and cooperative actions add further responses. The same starting weapons can therefore support different approaches as enemies and bosses change.

cards.heading: Complexity must remain readable
cards.text: Ikaruga's ship switches between black and white polarities, absorbing bullets of the matching colour. Collected energy powers a special attack, while destroying three consecutive enemies of one colour builds a score chain. The colour of an approaching shot determines whether it can be absorbed or must be avoided. Reading those distinctions remains essential as the screen fills.

main.title: Lunar: The Silver Star
main.subtitle: A boy who dreams of dragons
main.summary: Lunar: The Silver Star is Game Arts and Studio Alex's role-playing adventure, first released for Mega-CD in Japan on 26 June 1992.

cards.heading: A boy who dreams of dragons
cards.text: Lunar: The Silver Star is Game Arts and Studio Alex's role-playing adventure, first released for Mega-CD in Japan on 26 June 1992. Alex, a boy who admires the legendary Dragonmaster Dyne, leaves his small town on an adventure that grows into a struggle for Lunar's future. Companions join him as he explores settlements and dangerous places, learns about the dragons and works towards his own place in that history. The CD format gives the journey animated scenes, spoken passages and recorded music, adding another presence to its illustrated fantasy world.

cards.heading: Distance inside a turn-based battle
cards.text: Battles occur during exploration and use turn-based commands, with the characters' speed determining when actions take place. Position also matters: a fighter must reach an enemy to strike, while ranged attacks can cross that distance. The player can move a character, hold ground or retreat, making the battlefield more than a list of opposing statistics. Weapons and equipment found along the route improve the party's effectiveness. Experience from victories strengthens the group, allowing it to face the increasingly dangerous creatures encountered as Alex's journey reaches further from home.

cards.heading: A voice for the adventure
cards.text: Artist Toshiyuki Kubooka designed the characters, while Noriyuki Iwadare, Hiroshi Fujioka and Isao Mizoguchi contributed the music. Short animated and audio interludes give important moments another form alongside the ordinary conversations and exploration. Working Designs localised the game for North America in 1993, bringing that CD-based presentation to an English-speaking audience. Its success established the Lunar series before Eternal Blue continued the world in another era. The original's central appeal joins a familiar coming-of-age adventure to the sound and moving images that the new disc hardware could place around its characters.

main.title: Soldier Blade
main.subtitle: Seven operations at full speed
main.summary: Soldier Blade is Hudson's vertically scrolling shooter, first released for PC Engine on 10 July 1992.

cards.heading: Seven operations at full speed
cards.text: Soldier Blade is Hudson's vertically scrolling shooter, first released for PC Engine on 10 July 1992. The player's spacecraft crosses seven operations against the invading Zeograd Army, moving between formations, large enemies and bosses. Colored capsules provide different weapons, allowing the ship's fire to change as the action advances. Its emphasis on speed makes each approaching pattern a quick decision about position and firepower, while the clear weapon system lets the player read the consequences of collecting the next capsule immediately.

cards.heading: A weapon held in reserve
cards.text: The available weapons include a spreading Vulcan shot, a wave gun and a laser. Power-ups also bring a supporting pod, and up to three items can be stored for later use. Spending a weapon unleashes a powerful special attack, making the reserve a way to respond when the screen becomes dangerous. Taking damage can reduce the ship's strength, so collecting and preserving power remains part of the challenge. Bosses and intermediate encounters interrupt the scrolling stages with larger targets whose weak points must be reached through the surrounding fire.

cards.heading: A shooter built for the Caravan
cards.text: The project grew from planning for Hudson's Caravan tournament, and two-minute and five-minute score modes sit beside the main campaign. They condense the shooting into a repeatable contest over a fixed span of time. Designer Uriko Uribo worked under a short production schedule, while Keita Hoshi and Makiko Tanifuji composed the soundtrack. Yuji Kaida created the cover illustration. The finished game connects a full seven-stage journey with the tournament tradition of learning a short sequence closely enough to improve its score on the next attempt.

main.title: Mario Paint
main.subtitle: Mario Paint Turns the Super Famicom into a Creative Tool
main.summary: On July 14, 1992 Nintendo released Mario Paint for Super Famicom in Japan.

cards.heading: Mario Paint Turns the Super Famicom into a Creative Tool
cards.text: Nintendo released Mario Paint for the Super Famicom in Japan on July 14, 1992. Packaged with a mouse, it offers tools for drawing, short animations and musical sequences. Familiar Mario and Nintendo images appear as stamps, sounds and playful controls. Hidden title-screen animations and an insect-swatting game also give users reasons to practise the mouse.

cards.heading: Drawing and animation
cards.text: The drawing board offers 15 colours and 75 patterns, with pens, an airbrush, fills, lines, rectangles and circles. Parts of a picture can be copied, pasted, moved or flipped. Animation Land uses the same tools to build animations of four, six or nine frames, and the mouse can record a path for an animated object to follow. A separate stamp editor lets users alter existing stamps or draw their own.

cards.heading: Music written with icons
cards.text: The music composer represents sounds with familiar icons: Mario's head plays piano, a Power Star rings like a bell, and a Game Boy produces a pulse wave. Notes are placed on a treble clef. Compositions use common or triple time, with no sharps or flats and no more than three notes on a beat. Finished pieces can accompany animations and the colouring book.

cards.heading: Learning the mouse through play
cards.text: The title screen and Gnat Attack help players learn the SNES Mouse. Clicking the letters and scenery on the title screen triggers hidden animations. In Gnat Attack, the player swats 100 insects before fighting King Watinga. Its three levels repeat with faster enemies, turning precise pointing into a game of its own.
